issues.legal_issue: A life insurance policy may be challenged after two years when the policyholder fraudulently suppresses material facts known to them, and the two-year period runs from the policy’s original effective date rather than its revival.
material_facts: The insured answered negatively when asked whether he had consulted a medical practitioner within the preceding five years, although he had recently received treatment for serious ailments.
The insured also failed to disclose ailments including anaemia and shortness of breath in the accompanying personal statement.
The insurer repudiated the claim more than two years after the policy was originally effected, although the policy had been revived in the meantime.
The Court found that the insured knew the treatment and ailments were material to disclose and deliberately concealed them.
issues.conclusion: The conditions for challenging the policy under the second part of Section 45 of the Insurance Act, 1938 were satisfied. The two-year period ran from the date the policy was originally effected, not its revival, and the insurer was entitled to avoid the policy.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, 1938, after two years from the date a life policy is effected, an insurer may still call it in question if it proves that a statement concerned a material matter or suppressed facts material to disclose, that the suppression was fraudulent, and that the policyholder knew the statement was false or the facts were material to disclose. The period is calculated from the original date the policy was effected. The Court applied Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, under which fraud includes suggesting as true a fact that is not believed to be true and actively concealing a fact known to the party.

rule.if: life_policy_claim_repudiated and repudiation_more_than_two_years_after_original_effect and material_fact_suppressed and suppression_fraudulent and policyholder_knew_fact_was_material

predicates.life_policy_claim_repudiated: An insurer repudiated a claim made under a life insurance policy.
predicates.repudiation_more_than_two_years_after_or: The insurer repudiated the claim more than two years after the policy was originally effected, whether or not the policy was later revived.
predicates.material_fact_suppressed: The policyholder omitted a fact that was material to disclose when applying for the policy.
predicates.suppression_fraudulent: The policyholder deliberately concealed the fact or made a statement they did not believe to be true.
predicates.policyholder_knew_fact_was_material: The policyholder knew when making the statement or omission that the fact was material to disclose.

issues.definition: When a life insurance claim is repudiated more than two years after the policy was originally effected, the insurer may avoid the policy if the policyholder fraudulently suppressed a fact they knew was material to disclose.

issues.legal_issue: An insurer is not barred from challenging a life insurance policy merely because it medically examined the applicant if it lacked knowledge of the treatment fraudulently concealed by the applicant.
material_facts: The applicant was examined by several doctors at the insurer’s direction before the policy was issued and revived.
The insurer had reports about the applicant’s health, but had no means of knowing that he had been treated for serious ailments by another doctor.
The proposal and personal statement made the applicant’s health representations the basis of the contract, and the concealed treatment bore on the insurer’s consent.
issues.conclusion: The insurer was not estopped from challenging the policy, and the applicant could not rely on the Explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; no waiver arose on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the Explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872: a false representation is irrelevant if it did not induce the other party to enter into the contract. That principle did not assist the claimant because the insurer lacked knowledge of the concealed treatment, the health statements formed the basis of the contract, and the concealment bore on consent. The Court found no waiver. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

rule.if: life_policy_challenge_dispute and insurer_examined_applicant and insurer_lacked_knowledge_of_concealed_treatment and health_statements_formed_contract_basis and concealment_bore_on_insurer_consent

predicates.life_policy_challenge_dispute: A dispute concerns an insurer’s challenge to the validity of a life insurance policy.
predicates.insurer_examined_applicant: The insurer arranged for the applicant to undergo medical examinations.
predicates.insurer_lacked_knowledge_of_concealed_tr: The insurer did not know and had no means of knowing about treatment the applicant concealed.
predicates.health_statements_formed_contract_basis: The applicant’s health statements formed the basis of the insurance contract.
predicates.concealment_bore_on_insurer_consent: The concealed health information was relevant to the insurer’s decision to enter into the contract.

issues.definition: An insurer that examined an applicant is not barred from challenging the policy if it lacked knowledge of concealed treatment and the concealment concerned health statements that formed the basis of its consent.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant under a life insurance policy vitiated by the insured’s fraudulent suppression cannot recover premiums where the policy provides that paid money belongs to the insurer in that circumstance.
material_facts: The policy provided that money paid under it would belong to the insurer if the policy was vitiated by the insured’s fraudulent suppression of material facts.
The insured fraudulently suppressed material facts, and the claimant sought return of money paid to the insurer under the policy.
The claimant claimed under an assignment from the insured.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to a refund of the money paid. Sections 64 and 65 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 did not apply to the contract in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the policy term allocating paid money to the insurer if the policy was vitiated by fraudulent suppression. It also applied the principle that a court will not entertain an action for money had and received where the claimant must prove their own fraud to succeed. Where a contract stipulates that the other party is discharged from performance because of a breach of warranty, Sections 64 and 65 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 do not apply.

rule.if: claim_for_premium_refund and claimant_claims_under_fraudulent_insured and policy_vitiated_by_fraudulent_suppression and policy_allocates_paid_money_to_insurer_on_fraud

predicates.claim_for_premium_refund: A claimant seeks repayment of money paid under an insurance policy.
predicates.claimant_claims_under_fraudulent_insured: The claimant seeks recovery under the rights of an insured who fraudulently suppressed material facts.
predicates.policy_vitiated_by_fraudulent_suppressio: The policy was vitiated because the insured fraudulently suppressed material facts.
predicates.policy_allocates_paid_money_to_insurer_o: The policy provides that money paid under it belongs to the insurer if fraudulent suppression vitiates the policy.

issues.definition: A claimant seeking repayment under a policy cannot recover premiums if the claim derives from an insured whose fraudulent suppression vitiated a policy that allocates paid money to the insurer in that event.
